This Week in Democracy: A Slush Fund Dies, a Detention Center Erupts, and the Courts Split on Voting Rights

Bipartisan resistance killed a $1.8 billion presidential compensation fund, but a Supreme Court reversal on Alabama's map and violent crackdowns at a New Jersey detention facility showed how uneven the week's gains really were.

```markdown This was a week that seemed, for its first two days, like a run of genuine institutional pushback — and then spent the rest of its length demonstrating how quickly such gains can be undone, hedged, or quietly abandoned. Courts blocked a discriminatory map and a cultural-institution takeover. Congress forced a retreat on a $1.8 billion compensation fund. And yet by Friday, the map was back, the fund's fate was murkier than officials had claimed, and federal prosecutors were watching California count its votes while the president declared fraud before the count was finished.

The weekend set the pattern of courts asserting limits on executive power. A three-judge panel in Alabama, including two Trump appointees, unanimously found that the state's congressional map had been drawn with intentional discrimination against Black voters. That same weekend, a federal judge ruled that the Kennedy Center could not be renamed without congressional approval and blocked a planned two-year closure of the institution — prompting Trump to threaten to hand it back to Congress entirely and to launch a lengthy public attack on the judge who ruled against him. A third case added to the weekend's judicial scrutiny: a federal judge in Miami reopened Trump's $10 billion IRS lawsuit after 35 former federal judges alleged that the underlying settlement — which included a bar on auditing Trump's taxes and the creation of the $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization" fund — was the product of collusion. The judge ordered a response by June 12 and signaled that DOJ officials, including the acting attorney general, could be compelled to testify.

The weekend's other defining story began at Delaney Hall, a New Jersey ICE facility, where roughly 300 detainees had launched a hunger and labor strike over conditions inside. DHS denied any problems existed. Then came pepper spray, deployed against detainees and, notably, against a visiting senator. Governor Sherrill deployed state police, and the response escalated further into teargas and mounted units against protesters outside the facility. A journalist covering the demonstrations reported being directly targeted with a flash-bang — something he said he had never experienced in years of covering similar protests. Alongside these major threads, Capitol Police officers who had defended the building on January 6 sued to block the weaponization fund on constitutional grounds, while more than a dozen Republican senators privately pushed to kill it, worried about political exposure ahead of the midterms. Smaller stories rounded out the weekend: an OMB proposal to let political appointees terminate university research grants outside peer review, and a cluster of reporting on federal contracts and loans flowing toward companies tied to Trump and his family, including a $9.7 billion Pentagon contract to Dell awarded after Trump personally bought and promoted the company's stock.

By Monday, the Supreme Court delivered a narrower kind of relief. In a 6-3 ruling, the Court struck down Trump's executive order attempting to deny citizenship to children born to undocumented or temporary-visa parents, preserving a constitutional principle affecting more than 250,000 children a year. But three conservative justices dissented, lending unusual credibility to fringe legal theories and signaling that birthright citizenship's constitutional footing, while intact, was not secure. The same day, a federal appeals court found the Pentagon's transgender military ban likely unconstitutional and driven by animus, protecting currently serving members even as new enlistment remained barred, and a separate federal judge blocked the administration's attempt to move a major atmospheric research supercomputing center out of Colorado, ruling it was likely retaliation tied to a dispute with the state's governor. Also on Monday, the administration announced — for the first time — that it was abandoning the $1.8 billion weaponization fund, following a meeting between Trump and Speaker Johnson. Senate Democrats introduced the "Drain the Slush Fund Act" to make the reversal permanent and retroactive, a sign that they did not trust the announcement to hold on its own. Elsewhere, the Pentagon reclassified its press office in a way that barred journalists without appointments, and Trump posted language announcing a Washington rally nearly identical to his December 2020 call that preceded January 6, alongside AI-generated images depicting himself in grandiose and racially charged terms.

Tuesday brought the fund saga into open congressional testimony. Acting Attorney General Todd Blanche told Congress the Justice Department would not proceed with the fund, declaring it over "period" — but he declined to commit to that reversal in writing, an omission that would matter later in the week. House Republicans moved separately to block the fund and shelved $1 billion in White House ballroom security funding. The same day, Trump signed an executive order directing that bank accounts allegedly used to enable illegal immigration or store benefits be shut down, their funds seized and returned to taxpayers, framed as retaliation against "anti-ICE rioters." Separately, investigations revealed a network of purportedly progressive super PACs, funded through shell companies and vendors tied to House Republican leadership, coordinating to boost weak Democratic candidates and attack strong ones across multiple primary races. New Jersey's governor, attorney general, and Newark's mayor announced lawsuits against GEO Group over health conditions at Delaney Hall and the denial of state health department access — a distinct legal track from the protest-suppression story unfolding at the facility's gates. In a quieter admission, the administration cut tariffs on farm and construction equipment from 25 to 15 percent, tacitly conceding that tariffs had been driving up consumer prices after months of denying it.

Wednesday delivered the week's sharpest reversal. In an unsigned 6-3 decision, the Supreme Court overturned the prior weekend's lower-court finding on Alabama, permitting the state to use its redrawn map — the one found to intentionally discriminate against Black voters — for the midterms. The three liberal justices dissented sharply, accusing the majority of abandoning the rule of law. The whiplash was stark: a unanimous panel including two Trump appointees had found intentional discrimination just days earlier, and the nation's highest court erased that finding before the week was out. The same day, the House passed a war powers resolution 215-208, with four Republicans joining Democrats, directing Trump to end hostilities with Iran absent congressional authorization — the first such resolution to pass after months of blocked attempts, and only after Speaker Johnson had earlier tried to send members home early to prevent the vote. Trump signed a separate order stripping civil service protections from an estimated 8,000 to 10,000 senior federal employees, enabling their removal without due process — a restoration of a Project 2025 priority that had been rescinded under the previous administration. Trump also posted demanding that his New York criminal conviction and civil fraud judgment be dismissed, calling for the prosecution of Attorney General Letitia James and District Attorney Alvin Bragg. In smaller but pointed moments, the Senate parliamentarian ruled that ballroom security funding violated budget rules, forcing its removal from a reconciliation bill, and Representative Ted Lieu played footage during a House hearing showing Trump asleep in Cabinet meetings — footage Secretary Rubio denied witnessing despite sitting beside the president in it.

Thursday showed the Kennedy Center complying with the earlier court order, its general counsel directing staff to restore the institution's original name on signage by the following Friday — the clearest sign all week that judicial authority still carried practical weight somewhere. But the day's darker story came out of Louisiana, where Mamuka Artmeladze, 43, a detainee with no criminal record, was found unresponsive and pronounced dead at Winn Correctional Center. It was the 50th death in ICE custody under this administration and the 19th of the year, occurring after federal inspectors had already documented unsanitary conditions and excessive force at the facility. Separately, reporting found that fourteen of twenty-seven known corporate donors to Trump's White House ballroom project had secured new or expanded federal contracts worth more than $50 billion since donating, including Lockheed Martin, Amazon, Microsoft, Google, and Palantir. Trump also touted a "Trump Promenade" addition to the Lincoln Memorial without disclosing its funding, and described the ballroom project as incorporating a "DronePort" and other military elements. Oil reserves, meanwhile, fell to their lowest level since 2004, as the administration drained the Strategic Petroleum Reserve to manage price spikes tied to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz amid the ongoing Iran conflict. Governor Sherrill announced a $12 million increase in immigration legal defense funding, a modest concession following weeks of protest pressure over the state's Delaney Hall response.

Friday closed the week with the weaponization fund's fate still genuinely unresolved. The Senate passed a $70 billion ICE and Border Patrol funding package, 52-47, through reconciliation, funding immigration enforcement through the end of Trump's term — but every amendment aimed at restricting the anti-weaponization fund had failed the day before, leaving it technically alive despite the acting attorney general's public claim that it was dead. As California's gubernatorial primary count continued, Trump declared a premature winner and accused the state of rigging the election without evidence; the Justice Department sent a federal prosecutor to observe ballot processing in Los Angeles County and announced unspecified fraud investigations, which state officials rejected outright. A federal judge struck down a Trump policy that had frozen immigration benefit processing for nationals of 39 countries, calling it impermissible animus — even as, in a separate and unrelated case over the White House ballroom, DOJ lawyers argued that courts lacked authority to halt the project's construction even if it violated the law, comparing judicial intervention to an inability to stop the demolition of the Statue of Liberty. At a Florida detention facility, detainees reported that guards withheld food and provided contaminated water to pressure them into signing documents in English they could not understand, and ICE's acting director quietly rescinded a requirement to report detainee deaths occurring within 30 days of release — following a year that had already recorded dozens of such deaths. New York's legislature approved a one-year moratorium on large-scale data centers pending the governor's signature, and senior U.S. officials, including Vice President Vance, used a British murder case to promote anti-immigration messaging abroad.

Taken as a whole, the week offers a study in how quickly institutional wins can be reversed, hedged, or left ambiguous even as they are announced. Courts blocked a discriminatory map, only to have the Supreme Court restore it days later. Congress forced a public retreat on a contested compensation fund, only for the Senate to leave it technically intact and for the president to keep advocating for it after his own attorney general declared it over. A cultural institution complied with a judicial order to restore its name, even as the Justice Department argued in a separate case that courts had no power to stop a president's construction project at all. Detainees at one facility faced escalating force from state and federal agents; detainees at another died after documented warnings went unheeded, while the agency responsible quietly narrowed its own reporting obligations. None of these threads resolved cleanly by Friday. What the week recorded, more than any single verdict, was the persistent gap between institutions asserting their authority and the administration's capacity — sometimes successful, sometimes not — to outlast, evade, or simply ignore that assertion. ```
